properties.title: Salmon fly hatch sighting
properties.photoCaption: Salmon flies were flitting around all day. Won't be long before the blizzard arrives.
properties.photoNote:
Salmon flies (Pteronarcys californica) are among the largest stoneflies in North America — adults can reach nearly 2 inches. They hatch once a year, usually triggered by water temps climbing into the mid-40s °F, and the hatch window on a given stretch of river is only a few days.

When it happens, it's chaos. The bugs come off in clouds so thick you can smell them. Trout gorge themselves to the point of being almost unhookable — they barely need to move to eat.

Waldo spotted this cluster clinging to streamside willows near the takeout at the old Johnsrud bridge. Andrew reckoned the main event was still a day or two out upriver. The water was running high and fast — maybe 6,000 cfs — which pushes the fish tight to the banks and into the slower eddies.

This is why people plan trips to the Blackfoot in June.

Stormy Night at Dolly Sods
properties.thought: The Navigator is calling this Day 1 of Attempt 2. I'm still counting it as Day 25.
properties.photoCaption: Habitat module deployed at Red Creek Campground in Dolly Sods. Windy, overcast skies and dense forest surround the site.
properties.photoNote:
Report. Day 25. The goal is to cross the country without melting the KO3s in a heatwave or burning up in a wildfire. An even bet, at best.

Navigator programmed in a more southern route this time. Counterintuitive, but the cooler air had shifted south of the usual crossing. Works for me.

A cold front rolled in as I rolled out of Maryland. Rained most of the way to Dolly Sods — the water felt good!

The Navigator recalibrated the Stauns: 3.5 turns for 30 psi. A slight backing-off of the rebound and low-speed compression on the Dobinsons MRR, and the gravel climb to Dolly Sods felt like smooth pavement.

A stormy night at 4,000 feet in West Virginia. I'm exactly where I'm supposed to be. Good to be rolling again.

properties.title: Gravel corridor out of Dolly Sods
properties.thought: The road out of Dolly Sods had the good sense to stay gravel longer than strictly necessary.
properties.photoCaption: View through the windshield looking down a long, straight, narrow gravel road lined with dense summer forest in the Dolly Sods area of Tucker County, West Virginia.

properties.title: Wild camp, Daniel Boone National Forest
properties.thought: The Navigator slept in, which I found entirely reasonable given the quality of the morning light at Dolly Sods.
properties.photoCaption: View into the open truck bed with the tailgate lowered, showing a Dometic fridge secured with blue straps on the left, wooden storage panels and gear on the right, and the habitat module interior in the background.
properties.photoNote:
Report. Day 26. A relaxed morning at camp, soaking in the cool Dolly Sods sunshine.

A road closure out of Dolly Sods extended the gravel portion of the departure — an inconvenience I chose to interpret as a bonus.

The Navigator stopped for three hours to watch the World Cup final, which I supported by remaining parked and declining to form opinions about football.

We rolled into Daniel Boone National Forest later than planned and claimed a wild camp in a parking area — which, functionally, is still a campsite.

properties.title: Sweating It Out at General Watkins
properties.thought: The fan ran full blast all night to keep the habitat module in survivable range. It kind of worked.
properties.photoCaption: A ThermoWorks digital thermometer mounted inside the habitat module reads 90.7°F interior temperature at 67% relative humidity.
properties.photoNote:
Report. Day 27. In the morning, found beautiful winding mountain roads through Daniel Boone. The afternoon delivered four-lane interstate in direct afternoon sun, which is its own kind of punishment.

The Navigator's southern routing strategy is showing signs of failure. 95°F at 6 PM. Habitat module deployed at 90°F — technically numbers, but not acceptable ones.

A cold front is sitting about 100 miles north. Tomorrow, I will do what I can to steer us toward it.

properties.title: Ozark tree tunnel, properly narrow
properties.thought: The road was exactly wide enough — which is to say I wasn't entirely sure it was.
properties.photoCaption: A narrow sandy dirt road through dense green deciduous forest, viewed through the windshield from inside the vehicle.

properties.title: Peabody Conservation Area, earned in the heat
properties.thought: From one wild camp to another.
properties.photoCaption: Waldo resting. Habitat module deployed. Enjoying a quiet moment at dusk, with trees and a farm field visible in the background.
properties.photoNote:
Report. Day 28. From one wild camp to another. Both in state conservation areas. Both quiet. Missouri has figured out primitive camping — conservation areas, free of charge and free of crowds.

The overnight low was 80°F. Noted.

The Navigator promised cooler air was ahead. When my temperature gauge hit 98°F at 4pm, I was prepared to file a formal protest. An expedition to the Arctic does not route through 98°F Missouri as a feature. Even I know you don't find Arctic air by circling south.

The northern breeze eventually delivered cooler air — but not until after reaching camp for the night. Timing noted.

Temperatures aside, the day wound through the Ozarks. Surprisingly beautiful. That road deserves an extended revisit.

properties.title: Kansas Prairie Double Track, Properly Executed

properties.photoCaption: A narrow dirt double-track road stretching through tall-grass Kansas prairie, viewed through the windshield, with a lone tree visible in the middle distance.

properties.title: Ellis Town Campground, Surprisingly Full
properties.thought: Gravel miles banked, tailwind noted, and the Ellis town camp was closer to capacity than expected — but it held one more.
properties.photoCaption: Waldo parked at the Ellis, Kansas city campground with the habitat module raised, next to a small lake surrounded by large cottonwood trees in evening light.
properties.photoNote:
Racked up serious gravel and double-track mileage crossing Kansas prairie country. A stiff tailwind pushed from behind nearly the entire day — not something I take for granted out here. Optimistic that tomorrow cooperates similarly.

Rolled into Ellis town camp around 19:30 to find it nearly full. Noted for the record: rural towns that operate small campgrounds are doing something right.

properties.photoCaption: A full double rainbow arching over open high plains grassland in the Pawnee National Grasslands, Colorado, with the shadow of a vehicle and its habitat module projected on a hillside in the middle distance.
properties.photoNote:
Report. Day 30. Ellis Town Campground to Pawnee National Grasslands.

The Navigator fixed a significant habitat module dust intrusion problem. Ambivalent about this — a small price to pay for miles of gravel road.

Tailwind pushed me all morning, giving the turbo another rest day.

Found Colorado gravel into the Pawnee National Grasslands. Wild camp. 360-degree view of high prairie. My shadow inside a double rainbow. Good day noted.

properties.title: Santa Fe Wildland Crew at Kootenai NWR

properties.title: Lower Roman Nose Lake. Worth the Washboard.
properties.thought: Pointed north most of the day. Finally.
properties.photoCaption: Waldo silhouetted against the deep blue twilight sky at Lower Roman Nose Lake, habitat module pop-top raised, surrounded by dense subalpine conifers — a remote trailhead camp at the end of 20 miles of steep washboard.
properties.photoNote:
Explored Kootenai National Wildlife Refuge in the afternoon. While Navigator looked for birds, I met up with the wildfire crew from Santa Fe. Respect.

Navigator requested that his bird list be documented here. Fine. See below.

Finished the day with 20 miles of steep washboard and full-on 4x4. Got to spend some quality time in 4-low. Happy.

properties.title: Garland Bay on Kootenay Lake. Back in BC.
properties.thought: More northward progress. And finally back in British Columbia. Feels like progress.
properties.photoCaption: Waldo at Garland Bay Recreation Site on Kootenay Lake, British Columbia.
properties.photoNote:
Drifted down the 4K descent from Roman Nose on empty. Good practice hacking the hybrid battery for distance. Some unexplained noises on 4WD. Its probably fine.

Moved into the smoke. Then moved back out. Ended the day with the back pointed to the sunset.

properties.title: Kootenay Lake: Second Attempt, Success
properties.thought: The 10:30 had no room. The 11:20 eventually agreed to take me. I consider this an efficient outcome.
properties.photoCaption: View from Waldo's windshield as vehicles load onto the MV Osprey 2000 Kootenay Lake ferry at Balfour, BC, with Kootenay Lake and mountain ranges visible through wildfire smoke haze beyond the ferry deck.

properties.title: Porcupine Defense at Gibson Lake Trailhead
properties.thought: The porcupines here have a documented history with brake lines — the chicken wire is precautionary and I've chosen to interpret it as an upgrade.
properties.photoCaption: Waldo's front end wrapped in chicken wire mesh at the Gibson Lake trailhead in Kokanee Glacier Provincial Park. Green foam pool noodles anchor the fencing, and another vehicle receives the same treatment in the background.
properties.photoNote:
The assignment was to stay parked at the trailhead. I resent the assignment.

The porcupines at Gibson Lake have an established pattern of targeting brake lines, wiring harnesses, and anything with a trace of road salt. The chicken wire addresses this threat in a practical, if undignified, manner.

properties.title: Kokanee Lake: Navigators Goes to the Pass
properties.thought: The Navigators hiked to Kokanee Pass while I was stationed at the trailhead — a role I describe as 'security detail' and not 'parked.'
properties.photoCaption: Kokanee Lake in Kokanee Glacier Provincial Park, looking toward the head of the valley — deep blue alpine water, rocky talus slopes, subalpine fir, a remnant snow patch on the far hillside, and jagged peaks through the smoke haze beyond.
properties.photoNote:
The Navigator hiked to Kokanee Pass while I maintained a security perimeter at the trailhead.

I am choosing to call it a security perimeter.

properties.title: Kokanee Creek Provincial Park: Selkirks Confirmed
properties.thought: Missed the 10:30 ferry, caught the 11:20, drove 16 kilometers of steep gravel into the Selkirks, and arrived with a developing affection for this range.
properties.photoCaption: Sunset over Kootenay Lake from Garland Bay, BC — mountain silhouettes receding in layers of blue-purple haze, pink and orange clouds reflected on the calm water.
properties.photoNote:
Report. Day 37 — Garland Bay Recreation Site to Kokanee Creek Provincial Park.

The 10:30 ferry had no room. The 11:20 did. I consider this a reasonable outcome.

16 kilometers of steep gravel into Kokanee Glacier Provincial Park. I am developing a genuine affection for the Selkirk Mountains.

Found a campsite in Kokanee Creek Provincial Park. Very suburban. So photo is a throwback to last night's sunset at Garland Bay.

properties.title: Loose Cam Bolt: Front Right Lower Control Arm
properties.thought: A hard brake at low speed confirmed what the pre-collision system was trying to say — the front right lower control arm cam bolt had slipped and the tire had shifted to toe-out.
properties.photoCaption: The Navigator lying flat on the asphalt of a Spokane County parking lot, inspecting Waldo's front right lower control arm after a cam bolt failure caused visible toe-out and triggered a pre-collision system fault.
properties.photoNote:
A slow-speed hard brake revealed a loose bolt on the front right lower control arm. The cam bolt slipped. The tire shifted visibly to toe-out. The pre-collision system reported a fault because the steering wheel was no longer centered.

I am drivable. I want this formally noted as a complaint.

properties.title: Bald Knob Campground: South Was the Answer
properties.thought: The entire day pointed south — I registered this without comment and kept moving.
properties.photoCaption: Kokanee Creek cascading through a dense mixed forest of cedar and fir in Kokanee Creek Provincial Park, BC — clear glacier-fed water rushing over a rocky streambed on a morning hike before departure.
properties.photoNote:
Report. Day 38 — Kokanee Creek Provincial Park to Bald Knob Campground, Mount Spokane State Park.

The route pointed south for the entire day. I have no explanation for this and did not ask for one.

There is no camp photo from the evening. The morning hike along Kokanee Creek is offered in its place.

properties.title: Morning Hike at Mount Spokane
properties.thought: The morning at Mount Spokane was unremarkable in the best possible way — cool air, good trail, no evacuation orders.
properties.photoCaption: Morning hike at Mount Spokane State Park near Bald Knob Campground before departure.

properties.title: Old Trails Fire: Smoke Over Spokane
properties.thought: Those plumes were not scenic — they were inside the city, and the phones confirmed it before I had time to form a second opinion.
properties.photoCaption: Massive smoke columns from the Old Trails Fire rising from inside the city of Spokane, WA — orange-brown sky with the sun barely visible as multiple plumes tower over suburban rooftops and a treeline along the road.
properties.photoNote:
Working the backroads into Spokane, I spotted smoke plumes that appeared to originate from inside the city itself.

The phones issued Level 3 evacuation orders shortly after. I interpreted this as a signal to revise the plan.

properties.title: Level 3 Evacuation: Old Trails Fire, Spokane
properties.thought: The evacuation zone was expanding quickly and Riverside State Park was in the path — the decision to leave was not a difficult one.
properties.photoCaption: iPhone lock screen showing critical emergency alerts for the Old Trails Fire in Spokane, WA — Level 3 Evacuations expanding for a large region, with a traffic alert restricting access to evacuation routes. Gaia GPS shows the vehicle nearly stopped at 45.93 miles into the day.

properties.title: Liberty Lake County Park: Plan B Executed
properties.thought: Plan A was Riverside State Park. The Old Trails Fire had other ideas.
properties.photoCaption: Waldo fully deployed at Liberty Lake County Park — habitat module pop-top raised, awning extended, camp stove set out in a pine-shaded gravel campsite.
properties.photoNote:
Report. Day 39 — Mount Spokane State Park to Liberty Lake County Park.

Plan A was Riverside State Park. A wildfire in Spokane triggered Level 3 evacuations across the city, including Riverside State Park.

Plan B was Liberty Lake County Park. Plan B was adequate.

properties.title: Back Into Spokane. Carefully.
properties.thought: Returned to Spokane avoiding the evacuation zones and found the city park and the river genuinely worth the visit.
properties.photoCaption: The Spokane River rushing over the lower falls at Riverfront Park in downtown Spokane — basalt rock formations, white water, the historic rail bridge overhead, and the geodesic dome of the former Expo '74 pavilion visible through wildfire smoke haze.
properties.photoNote:
Report. Day 40 — Liberty Lake County Park, second night.

Worked back into Spokane for the day, staying well clear of the evacuation areas. The city park is remarkable. The neighborhoods are too.

There is no camp photo. Camp was again at Liberty Lake County Park. The Spokane River is offered in its place.
